R05-G-01: A familiar way of thinking about pollution treats it as a simple wrong: one party harms another, and the law should stop the harm or make the harmer pay. An influential argument in economics asks us to look at the situation differently. Suppose the smoke from a small factory soils the washing of a few households nearby. The harm, on this view, is reciprocal: to protect the washing is to restrict the factory, and to protect the factory is to burden the households. If the parties could bargain freely and cheaply, the argument runs, they would arrive at the efficient outcome whoever held the legal right. If the households had the right to clean air, the factory would pay them to tolerate some smoke whenever its gains exceeded their losses; if the factory had the right to emit, the households would pay it to fit a filter whenever the filter cost less than the damage it prevented. The conclusion is often summarised as a reason for governments to stand aside: define property rights clearly, and private bargaining will do the rest. That reading takes the conditional for the claim. The striking result holds only when bargaining is nearly costless, and the more interesting lesson lies in how rarely that condition is met. A few households and one factory can meet around a table. A city of several million people breathing the exhaust of a million vehicles cannot. Each resident's share of the harm is small, working out who caused how much of it is difficult, and every resident has a reason to let others negotiate and pay while enjoying the cleaner air for nothing. The costs of finding the parties, measuring the damage and enforcing an agreement swamp whatever gains the bargain might bring. Read in this way, the argument is less a case against regulation than a map of where it is needed. Where the parties are few, the harm is visible and agreements can be checked, private settlement may indeed work better than a rule imposed from outside; the neighbours of a noisy workshop may settle a dispute over evening hours more sensibly than any ordinance could. Where the parties are many and scattered, the same reasoning that praises bargaining in principle explains why it will not happen in practice, and why a tax, a standard or a tradable permit can stand in for a negotiation that no one is able to hold. None of this makes the assignment of rights a matter of indifference. Even when bargaining would reach the same physical outcome, it matters a great deal who pays whom. A rule that gives the factory the right to pollute leaves the households poorer by the price of their clean air; a rule that gives them the right leaves the factory's owners poorer instead. Efficiency may be blind to that difference. Those who live downwind are not.
R05-G-02: In 1865 the economist William Stanley Jevons argued that Britain's growing skill at burning coal efficiently would not conserve its coal but hasten its exhaustion. Cheaper steam power, he reasoned, would make steam worth using in trades that had never used it, and the extra demand would more than swallow the saving. The idea has enjoyed a curious afterlife in contemporary environmental argument. It is invoked today, often with a note of triumph, by those who doubt that better lamps, engines and insulation can do much for the climate. It is dismissed, often with equal confidence, by those who regard efficiency as the cheapest source of clean energy there is. Both camps tend to treat the question as if it had a single answer, when the size of the effect plainly depends on circumstances. The mechanism itself is not in dispute. When a service becomes cheaper to provide, people generally consume more of it, and the additional consumption offsets part of the anticipated reduction. A household that insulates its walls may heat more rooms, or keep them warmer; a driver whose car burns less fuel per kilometre may drive further, or buy a heavier car next time. Economists call the part of the expected saving that is eaten up in this way the rebound. What is disputed is its size. Where demand for a service is already close to saturation, as with lighting in a well-lit home, the rebound tends to be modest: few people want their rooms twice as bright merely because brightness has become cheap. Where energy is a basic input to production, and cheaper energy lets whole industries expand, the rebound can be large, and in the case Jevons studied it may well have exceeded the saving. There is also a subtler and less visible channel of transmission. Money saved on fuel does not vanish; it is spent on something else, and that something else uses energy too. A family that spends less on petrol may take a holiday flight it could not previously afford. These indirect effects are considerably harder to trace than the direct ones, which is one reason why published estimates of the total rebound vary so widely across studies and sectors. The sensible conclusion is neither that efficiency is futile nor that it is sufficient. Efficiency genuinely improves people's material circumstances: they obtain more warmth, light and travel for their money, and that is a gain in its own right. But if the aim is to reduce total energy use or emissions, efficiency works best when it is paired with something that keeps energy costly enough that the saving is not simply spent on using more of it, such as a tax on carbon or a cap on emissions. Efficiency then supplies the comfort, and the price makes sure that the comfort is not bought with the very fuel that was meant to be saved.
R05-G-03: Economists who agree that carbon emissions should carry a price often disagree, sometimes heatedly, about how the price should be set. One camp prefers a tax: the government announces a charge per tonne of emissions and leaves firms to decide how much to cut. The other prefers a cap with tradable permits: the government fixes the total quantity of emissions allowed, issues permits for that amount, and lets trading among firms determine what a permit costs. In a world without uncertainty the two would be equivalent. Any cap implies some price at which permits would trade, and any tax implies some level to which emissions would fall; a regulator who knew the costs of abatement could reach the same outcome by either route. The difference appears once we admit that no one knows those costs in advance. A tax fixes the price and leaves the quantity uncertain: if cutting emissions proves harder than expected, firms will pay the tax and emit more than was planned. A cap fixes the quantity and leaves the price uncertain: if cutting proves harder, permit prices will climb, perhaps steeply. Which uncertainty is more tolerable depends on the shape of the damage. If each additional tonne does roughly the same harm as the last, a fixed price tracks the damage well and a volatile price merely adds cost. If harm accelerates sharply past some threshold, a fixed quantity matters more than a stable price. Because the harm from carbon depends on the stock accumulated in the atmosphere over decades rather than on any single year's emissions, many economists conclude that year-to-year overshoots matter little and that a tax, or something that behaves like one, is the better instrument. Advocates of trading reply that this argument, persuasive in the seminar room, neglects politics. A cap states its environmental goal openly, which can make it easier to defend, and the free allocation of permits to affected industries, though it hands them a windfall, has often been the price of getting a scheme adopted at all. A tax, by contrast, announces a cost to every voter and invites a fresh campaign against it with every scheduled rise. The more telling fact is that, in practice, the two designs have drifted towards each other. Trading schemes have acquired price floors, to keep permits from becoming nearly worthless when demand falls, and price ceilings, to stop them from spiking; taxes have been given scheduled increases linked to emissions targets. The resulting hybrids are neither pure price nor pure quantity. This convergence suggests that the long debate was, in part, a debate about labels. What decides whether a carbon price works is less whether it is called a tax or a cap than whether it is high enough, broad enough in what it covers, and credible enough that firms invest on the expectation that it will last.
R05-G-04: Few proposals in environmental policy provoke as much unease as the suggestion that nature should be given a price. To put a figure in money on a wetland, a forest or a population of pollinating insects seems to many people a category mistake, as though one were to ask what a friendship is worth in rupees. Critics worry that once a forest has a price it can be sold, and that the language of valuation quietly concedes the very thing it was meant to resist: that everything can be exchanged for money. Defenders of valuation reply that the choice is not between pricing nature and refusing to. Every decision to drain a marsh for housing, or to leave it alone, already implies a valuation; it merely leaves the valuation unstated. When a planning authority approves a road through a forest because the time saved by drivers is worth a stated sum, and counts the forest as worth nothing because no one has put a figure on it, the forest has in effect been priced at zero. Making the value explicit, on this view, does not turn nature into a commodity but protects it from being treated as free. A wetland that absorbs floodwater does work that would otherwise require embankments and pumps, and the cost of those replacements is a reasonable, if rough, guide to what the wetland does for the town beside it. This reply seems to me largely right, but only within limits that its enthusiasts tend to forget. Valuation in money is a tool for comparing small changes: whether to drain this marsh or that one, whether to widen a road by a lane or route it elsewhere. It answers the question of what a little more or a little less of something is worth, given that most of it remains. It is far less suited to valuing whole systems on which economic life itself depends. To ask what all the pollinators in the world are worth is not like asking what one orchard's bees are worth and multiplying by the number of orchards. If the pollinators were gone, the prices used in the calculation, of fruit, of land, of labour, would themselves be different, and the figure would describe a world that no longer exists. Very large totals for the value of nature's services, however striking, should therefore be read as rhetoric rather than as accounts. The practical lesson is to use valuation where it is strong and to set limits where it is weak. For decisions at the margin, an explicit figure is better than an implicit zero. For losses that would be large, irreversible or system-wide, a rule that simply forbids them, such as a minimum area of forest or a floor on water quality, may serve better than any price, because the price would become meaningless at exactly the point where it mattered most.
R05-G-05: Imagine a middle-income country that discovers large reserves of natural gas off its coast. Export earnings surge, foreign currency pours in, and the national currency rises in value. For a while the effects look wholly benign: imports become cheaper, the government collects more revenue, and wages climb as the gas sector and the services that cater to it compete for workers. Yet a decade later the country's manufacturers, who sell abroad against foreign rivals, may find themselves in serious trouble. A stronger currency makes their goods dearer in foreign markets, and the higher wages set by the booming sectors raise their costs at home. Factories close or move away, and the economy comes to rest ever more heavily on a single commodity. The pattern is common enough to have a name, Dutch disease, taken from the experience of the Netherlands after its large gas discoveries. Some economists see nothing pathological in this. A country that finds itself rich in gas, they argue, should export gas and import the manufactures it once made, just as a country with fertile land should grow food. The movement of labour and capital out of factories is, on this account, the market reallocating resources to where they now earn most. To call it a disease is to mistake adjustment for illness. The argument is coherent, but it assumes that the sectors lost can be regained whenever conditions change, and that assumption is doubtful. Manufacturing is not merely one way among others of earning foreign exchange. It is a place where workers acquire skills, where firms learn by doing, and where suppliers, engineers and managers accumulate knowledge that exists in no manual. Such capabilities take years to build and decay quickly once the firms that hold them have gone. Gas, meanwhile, is finite, and its price is notoriously volatile. When the price falls or the fields run down, the currency weakens and exporting becomes profitable again in principle, but the firms, skills and networks that would have taken advantage of the change no longer exist. The country finds that it cannot simply return to where it was. The remedy, then, is not to leave the gas in the ground but to manage the boom so that it does not hollow out everything else. A government can save a large share of the windfall abroad, in a fund invested in foreign assets, which slows the rise of the currency and spreads the benefit across generations; it can spend at home at a pace the economy can absorb without bidding up wages across the board. Such measures are politically hard, because they ask citizens to forgo spending money they can see. But the alternative is to treat a temporary gift as permanent income, and to discover too late that the industries it displaced were not as replaceable as the theory assumed.
R05-G-06: National income statistics were designed to answer a question about production: how much an economy produces in a year. They were never meant to measure welfare, and some of those who built them said as much. But a statistic that is published every quarter, reported on the evening news and used to judge governments acquires a meaning beyond its design. Growth in gross domestic product has come to stand for success, and the blind spots of the measure have come to matter accordingly. One blind spot bears directly on the environment. When a country fells a forest and sells the timber, the sale counts as production, and nothing is subtracted for the forest that is no longer there. When a country pumps oil from its fields, the revenue counts as income, though the oil in the ground was an asset and its extraction leaves the country with less of it. A household that sold a piece of its furniture every year and described the proceeds as salary would be judged to have misunderstood its own finances. National accounts already make a version of the necessary correction for machines and buildings, deducting their wear to arrive at net product; the same logic, applied consistently, would deduct the depletion of forests, fisheries, minerals and soil. A second blind spot runs in the opposite direction. Spending that merely repairs damage counts as output. If a factory pollutes a river and the town downstream builds a treatment plant to make the water drinkable again, both the factory's production and the plant's construction add to GDP, though the town ends up with no more clean water than it had before the factory arrived. Defensive spending of this kind can make a deteriorating situation look like growth. It does not follow that GDP should be abandoned, as some of its critics urge. For the purposes it was designed to serve, such as tracking output and employment through booms and slumps, it remains indispensable, and no alternative matches its consistency across countries and decades. Nor are the corrections straightforward. Valuing the depletion of a fishery requires assumptions about future prices and about the rate at which the stock regenerates, and different assumptions yield very different answers. The more modest and more defensible proposal is to publish, alongside GDP, accounts that record changes in natural assets, so that a country that grows by drawing down its capital can at least be seen to be doing so. A figure that is imperfect but visible is likelier to change behaviour than a correct one that nobody computes.
R05-G-07: The quarrel between advocates of green growth and advocates of degrowth is usually staged as a dispute about a single empirical question: can economic output keep rising while the pressure it places on the planet falls? Green growth answers yes. Rich economies, it observes, have already shown that output and emissions can move apart, as electricity is generated from cleaner sources, heavy industry gives way to services, and the same goods are made with less material. Degrowth answers no, or not fast enough. Some of the apparent separation, it replies, reflects production moved abroad rather than pollution avoided; much of the rest is merely relative, a fall in emissions per unit of output that is swamped by the growth of output itself. On this view the only reliable way for rich countries to shrink their ecological footprint is to shrink their economies, or at least to stop enlarging them. Both sides are right about something, and the way they frame the dispute obscures what it is really about. That emissions and output can diverge in absolute terms is no longer a mere hypothesis; it has happened in a number of countries, even after allowing for the carbon embodied in their imports. But the existence of absolute decoupling settles less than its champions suppose. The relevant question is not whether emissions can fall while output rises but whether they can fall fast enough, given how little more carbon the atmosphere can absorb before the damage becomes severe. A rate of decline that would be impressive in almost any other context may still be far too slow in this one. Equally, the degrowth case proves less than its champions suppose. That past decoupling has been too slow does not show that it must remain so; the pace of change in energy technology has repeatedly surprised forecasters, and the costs of some forms of clean power have fallen faster than most people expected a generation ago. The deeper difficulty is that both camps take GDP as the variable of interest, one wishing to keep it rising and the other to see it fall. Yet GDP is neither the cause of environmental damage nor its cure. It is a sum of market transactions, some of which burn fuel and clear land and some of which, such as teaching, nursing or repairing, do very little of either. An economy could grow while its emissions fell sharply, if the growth came from activities of the second kind; it could shrink while its emissions rose, if a recession struck services harder than it struck heavy industry. To make the size of GDP the target, in either direction, is to aim at a proxy that is only loosely tied to the thing that matters. A more productive stance would be indifference to growth as such. Policy would set limits directly on what does harm, through carbon prices, caps on extraction and the protection of land, and then let output rise or fall as it will within those limits. Such a stance asks something uncomfortable of each side. Advocates of green growth would have to accept that if the limits prove binding, slower growth may be the price, and that this would be not a failure of policy but a possible result of it. Advocates of degrowth would have to accept that if the limits are met while output rises, there is no further environmental case for shrinking the economy, whatever other reasons they may have for wanting a different kind of society. Neither concession is trivial, which may explain why the debate is so seldom conducted on these terms.
R05-G-08: A country that puts a serious price on carbon faces an awkward possibility. If its steelmakers, cement works and chemical firms must pay for their emissions while their competitors abroad do not, production may move to places where emitting is free. The country's own emissions fall, but the world's do not, and some of its industry has been lost for nothing. Economists call this leakage, and fear of it has been among the most effective arguments against acting alone. The obvious answer is a border adjustment: a charge on imports equal to the carbon price that would have been paid had the goods been made at home, perhaps paired with a rebate for exporters. Domestic and foreign producers would then compete on equal terms, and the incentive to relocate would disappear. The proposal is simpler to state than to carry out. To charge an import for its carbon, one must know how much carbon went into making it, and that depends on the plant, the fuel it burned and the electricity grid it drew from, none of which an importing government can observe directly. Default values can be assigned by product and by country, but these penalise clean producers in dirty countries and reward dirty producers in clean ones. Letting producers prove their actual emissions instead requires inspectors or trusted certifiers inside the exporting country, which raises questions of sovereignty as well as of cost. Trading partners, moreover, are apt to see the charge as protection dressed in green, and some have a further complaint: that countries which grew rich by burning carbon for two centuries are now taxing the goods of countries trying to do the same, and calling it fairness. There is also reason to think the problem itself has been overstated. For most industries the cost of carbon is a small share of total costs beside labour, transport, access to markets and the quality of local institutions, and firms do not move plants lightly. A steelworks embodies decades of investment in a site, a workforce and a web of local suppliers, and escaping a modest carbon price would seldom justify abandoning all of that. The evidence from carbon prices so far suggests less relocation than the warnings predicted, though the prices in question have mostly been modest and some heavy industries have been shielded from them by free allowances, so the past may be a poor guide to the effect of prices high enough to matter. If leakage is less of a threat than feared, why does the border adjustment matter? Its most important effect may lie not in the trade it reshapes but in the decisions it prompts elsewhere. An exporting country whose firms face a charge at the border has a reason to prefer that its own government levy an equivalent price at home, so that the revenue stays at home instead of flowing to a foreign treasury. A border adjustment can thus act less as a wall than as a lever, drawing other countries towards carbon pricing of their own. Whether it does so, or instead provokes retaliation, depends heavily on how it is designed and presented. A charge that credits carbon prices already paid abroad, that measures actual emissions where producers can show them, and that directs some of its revenue to helping poorer exporters cut their emissions has a chance of being accepted as what it claims to be. One that does none of these things will be read, not unreasonably, as the protectionism its critics allege.
